Two container ships sink near strait of Hormuz amid surge in Iranian attacks
Vessels were hit by missiles as rise in strikes suggests Iran is trying to close waterway before US midterm elections
Two container ships near the strait of Hormuz have ⁠sunk after being struck by missiles, amid the sharpest rise in Iranian attacks on shipping since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran .
The increase in attacks suggests Iran is trying to fully close the strategic waterway in an attempt to frustrate Donald Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The Trump administration has been attempting to deflect attention from the economic impact of the war on Iran by blaming Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries for increased fuel prices.
On Wednesday, UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported at least five incidents including drone strikes in the previous 48 hours targeting tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area.
“There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said.
The Singapore-flagged ​container ‌ship GFS Pride sank on Wednesday after an attack the previous day. Hours later, the Antigua- and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, having been hit by a ​projectile ​on 23 September, according to data from ‌the ‌International Maritime Organization.
Apparently referring to the GFS Pride, Iran said a cargo ship had sunk after hitting a naval mine while making an unauthorised passage through the strait.
State television quoted a statement from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that said the ship was travelling on an “illegal and dangerous route” when it hit the mine.
The ship, which was shown tilted in the water and spewing a thick plume of smoke, was carrying 2,500 containers, the broadcast said.
Vessels in the strait of Hormuz near Bandar Abbas, Iran. UKMTO reported at least five incidents including drone strikes in the previous 48 hours. Photograph: Razieh Poudat/Reuters However, UKMTO suggested that both ships had been hit by unidentified projectiles, raising questions over Tehran’s account.
Iran has repeatedly warned ships against trying to transit through the strait without its approval. The US military has been guiding ships through the waterway on a route nearer to Oman’s coast.
Ships in the area were reporting an intense series of attacks in recent days, with six vessels attacked on Sunday alone, according to UKMTO’s monitoring.
Analysis by the Financial Times said 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to 11 October. Of the vessels hit, three were refined energy product tankers and two others were crude oil tankers.
The increased tempo of Iranian attacks appears to have caused a dramatic drop-off in oil shipments through the strait, as Tehran appears determined to demonstrate its ability to strike ships before the US midterms that will decide control of Congress.
US fuel prices have surged by almost 70% since Trump launched his war on Iran, and the Republican party is bracing for punishment at the polls.
US fuel prices have surged by almost 70% since Donald Trump launched his war on Iran. Photograph: Bizuayehu Tesfaye/Las Vegas Review-Journal/AP According to two Iranian officials, Iran has recently begun using new tactics against vessels it considers to be in violation of its restrictions. The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being ⁠to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.
“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials told Reuters.
The decision to adopt the new ​strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ‌ruling system, the officials added.
A US military official, ‌speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Tehran had changed tactics in one significant way. After the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the IRGC had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to ‌identify potential targets, including American naval vessels, the official said.
Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.

items.content:
Ukrainian military’s access to Starlink satellite internet suddenly restricted
Launch of Russian ballistic missiles on Ukraine, with no US warning, coincides with outage of Starlink managed by Musk’s SpaceX
Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.
The terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the terminals travelling at high speeds on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Donald Trump has denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine . Zelenskyy also indicated that the US was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine in an interview with NPR aired on Wednesday, but confirmed that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited.
Ukraine did not receive any warning before Russia launched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening, according to Col Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the air force. But it did receive warnings from “foreign partners” about three subsequent barrages, leaving further confusion about whether or not the US is intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine.
Musk said that Starlink is not licensed to clients who are using weapons, and that the Ukrainian military was linked to a separate network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government. “This is not under SpaceX control,” Musk wrote.
Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
A firefighter works at the site of a food store hit by a Russian attack on Lutsk on 14 October. Photograph: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/Reuters Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.
“With their actions our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.
But there have been no reports that access for static Starlink terminals has been cut, meaning critical battlefield communications for soldiers should remain unaffected. The detection of incoming Russian missiles and drones relies on other technologies.
Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader – an extraordinary act of political interference against a wartime ally – as a personal feud between the two presidents has burst into the open.
The reports that Starlink was being throttled on the frontlines were interpreted by some as further pressure on Ukraine to end the fighting and make a deal with Russia at any cost.
Serhii Sternenko, a political activist with close ties to the military, first reported the outage and later said that the speeds at which the loss of connectivity occurred had fallen even lower. “It is likely that the company ‘SpaceX’ resorted to such measures at the request of the Trump administration,” he said. “Ordinary satellite communication terminals are currently operational.”
Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy decries ‘absolutely unjust’ lack of warning from allies after Kyiv plant strike
Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
Zelenskyy had suggested, though not said, that the US was intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine about impending Russian missile strikes.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” Zelenskyy said. “Russia does not consider the American president’s statements strong.”
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become even more widespread.
Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed by either side. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”
Ukraine is observing a short-term moratorium on striking Russian refineries while Kyiv seeks to show that it is ready for talks with Russia. Zelenskyy arrived in London on Wednesday to meet Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister. He will also be received by King Charles.
Zelenskyy is seeking new negotiations with the US. He has sent proposals to the Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, saying Ukraine was ready to work towards a ceasefire and “Russia must also be part of this agreement”.

Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham matters Close
Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed President Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday, as the Ukrainian leader looks to shore up his European allies five years into Russia's war on Ukraine.
Burnham told Zelensky that Britain "would forever stand by you" and that he was accelerating the delivery of air defences to Ukraine.
Burnham previously told MPs that he would try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States and that Ukraine won't leave "empty-handed".
The two leaders met at No 10 Downing Street where Zelensky was welcomed with a military ceremonial guard - thought to be a first for a foreign leader.

Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz as Iran steps up attacks
The GFS Pride, registered in Singapore, sank after it was struck by an unidentified projectile and caught fire.
The ship's 21 crew members were safely evacuated and no injuries have been reported, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore.

Amos Hochstein on Iran war latest: I've stopped understanding what the U.S. strategy is
A container ship sank in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday as Iran escalated its attacks on commercial vessels.
The GFS Pride, registered in Singapore, sank after it was struck by an unidentified projectile and caught fire. The ship's 21 crew members were safely evacuated and no injuries were reported, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore .
"Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law," the Singapore maritime authority said in a statement Wednesday.
Containers were floating in the water after the vessel sank, Pakistani maritime authorities warned in a navigational alert . It is the third commercial ship sunk during the Iran war, according to the International Maritime Organization , a United Nations' agency.
A second Singapore-registered container ship, the GFS Giselle, sustained damage to its hull after it was hit by an unidentified projectile on Wednesday. The ship has arrived at safe anchorage and none of its crew were hurt, the Singapore maritime authority said.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed early Wednesday that a container ship exploded and sank after hitting a naval mine, according to the state news agency Tasnim . But there is no independent evidence to confirm that a mine is what caused the Pride to sink, according to the maritime security firm Marisks.
Iran's claims are "consistent with an ongoing psychological operations campaign aimed at generating fear, increasing uncertainty and discouraging commercial shipping" in Hormuz, Marisks said in a security alert.
Iran has escalated its strikes on commercial ships transiting Hormuz in recent weeks, as it tries to choke off a rebound in crude oil exports through the strait.
More than 20 vessels, mostly oil tankers, have come under attack this month in Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
The attacks this month have left two sailors missing and more than a dozen injured, according to the IMO.
Crude oil exports through Hormuz hit prewar levels in September as the U.S. military guided tankers through the strait, but shipments have since pulled back as attacks have increased. Oil prices closed slightly higher Wednesday.
Exports through Hormuz averaged 8.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in the week ended Oct. 12, nearly 40% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to data from Kpler .
Shipments from the Middle East, including pipelines to the Gulf of Oman and Red Sea, stood at 14 million bpd, or nearly 20% below prewar levels, the data showed.
Daily crude flows are very volatile, with only 3 million barrels of crude transiting Hormuz on Monday while 6 million barrels passed through the strait on Friday, according to Kpler.

items.content:
Ukraine raises alarm over Starlink limits disrupting military operations
For the second time this week, Ukraine didn't receive advance warning from partners of Russian ballistic missile attacks, President Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy's defense tech advisor Serhii Beskrestnov suggested limits on SpaceX's Starlink were to blame for the lack of advance warning.
Meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians are without power as of Wednesday morning after Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure overnight, despite Trump's "energy ceasefire."
Ukraine has accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its military-grade Starlink internet service without warning, disrupting Ukrainian military operations.
It comes as Russia intensifies attacks on the country's energy infrastructure despite President Donald Trump's proposed "energy ceasefire."
Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said Wednesday that SpaceX has implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion without notifying Ukrainian defense forces, disrupting some missions. The restrictions apply to the sister service Starshield, which supports national security.
Meanwhile, Russia unleashed an attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions, raising further questions about the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Sunday.
"There is significant damage to facilities and equipment – at 26 facilities of our power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector," Zelenskyy said in a post on X early Wednesday.
He highlighted a targeted ballistic missile strike against the energy infrastructure that Zelenskyy said should have been covered by the "energy ceasefire" announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday.
"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Zelenskyy said.
The attack comes after the Ukrainian president on Monday accused Russia of violating Trump's proposal that the adversaries stop attacking each other's energy facilities to help bring down the cost of oil and diesel.
Both Russian and Ukrainian authorities initially denied any knowledge of an energy ceasefire agreement. Ukraine has since welcomed such a deal, while Russian authorities said talks are ongoing, without confirming whether they have reached an agreement.
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday: "Regarding the status of this agreement, we can refer to Zelensky's reaction. When asked the same question, he said he had not heard of such an agreement, would welcome clarification and was ready for a ceasefire," according to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Zelenskyy also said that for the second time this week, Ukraine received no advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches. The latest unflagged strike on Kyiv damaged a residential building and killed one person and injured six, Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine's Beskrestnov said that the Starlink speed restriction currently applies to the Starshield military service package and is set at 100 mph, or about 160 km/h.
"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram. "SpaceX is likely to have taken such measures at the request of the Trump administration," he added in a separate post.
SpaceX and the White House didn't respond to requests for comment.

items.title: Diplomat Richard Haass discusses the Russia-Ukraine war and Trump's role - NPR
items.summary: Diplomat Richard Haass discusses the Russia-Ukraine war and Trump's role  NPR
items.content:
Diplomat Richard Haass discusses the Russia-Ukraine war and Trump's role NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with veteran diplomat Richard Haass about the Russia-Ukraine war and the role President Trump is playing.
Diplomat Richard Haass discusses the Russia-Ukraine war and Trump's role
Diplomat Richard Haass discusses the Russia-Ukraine war and Trump's role
< iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6000164/nx-s1-9963390" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with veteran diplomat Richard Haass about the Russia-Ukraine war and the role President Trump is playing.
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST: Richard Haass has been listening with us to Joanna's interview with Ukraine's president. Richard is president emeritus of the Council on Foreign Relations and was a principal adviser to the secretary of state during the George W. Bush administration. Mr. Haass, welcome back. RICHARD HAASS: Good to be with you, Steve. INSKEEP: What do you make of that revelation that the U.S. at least seems to have blocked some intelligence-sharing with Ukraine? HAASS: What I make of it is it's all too consistent with the pattern of U.S. foreign policy towards this war over the last year and a half. We have consistently done things for Russia, and we have consistently done things to Ukraine. And that is a - and this is simply the latest shoe to drop. INSKEEP: And how does this fit in with the president's effort to get diesel fuel out of Russia? HAASS: Well, the president made this deal to get a small amount of diesel fuel out of Russia. It will have negligible, if any, impact on the price of diesel, which is over $6.50 a gallon nationwide. It's up - what? - 70% since the Iran war began. And that's the bottom line. Diesel is sky-high. The price has spiked because of the president's war in Iran. But what he's doing instead is blaming the Ukrainians, who are attacking Russian energy infrastructure. It's one of the few things they can do to put any pressure on Russia in retaliation for their attacks. And what we've done is weakened economic sanctions and any pressure against Vladimir Putin. So again, it will have no impact on prices here, but it will have an impact on this war. INSKEEP: Why do you think it will have no impact on prices here? HAASS: As the cliche goes, it's a drop in the bucket. The amount of fuel that would come from Russia is less than a day's supply. It's just - you know, worldwide. It's just not going to make a difference. It will, however, make a difference to the Russian economy. And it does, once again, break sanctions, by the way, just days after the U.S. Congress finally passed a sanctions bill named for former Senator Lindsey Graham meant to increase pressure on Russia. INSKEEP: How striking is it that the president has been telling Ukraine or urging Ukraine not to go after Russian energy facilities, which is a tactic that seemed to have given Ukraine some success? HAASS: Well, it is quite striking. What is Ukraine meant to do? We've taken away their ability to defend themselves. We're not providing them Patriot air defense missiles and other systems. We've kind of burned through them in the Middle East. And we had stopped providing them directly, in any case, even before the Iran war. So Ukraine is increasingly defenseless. You added what seems to have happened last night - that we've stopped providing them some of the tactical intelligence about incoming missiles, so they can't ready their air defense systems. We seem to have also interrupted some of their ability to access Starlink, which interferes now then with their ability to send drones against Russia. So again, what we're doing is we're tying the hands of the victim here. Again, let's not forget, Steve, this is a war of Russian aggression. This is the second war of Russian aggression against Ukraine. There was 2014, where they took Crimea. There's this war, which is going on for - what? - four-plus years now. And yet this war is inconsistent with the most basic norm, the most basic principle of international relations - that territory is not to be acquired by force. Russia is violating it by the day, by the hour. And the United States, for reasons that are inexplicable to me, continues to embrace the aggressor and blame the victim. INSKEEP: OK. You said inexplicable, and yet I'm going to invite you to try to explain. HAASS: (Laughter). INSKEEP: Help me do a little reverse-engineering here. We've identified these various things the United States is doing to pressure Ukraine. When you look at the U.S. using its tools in that way and try to work backward as to what the rationale would be, what the motivation would be, what the reason would be, what do you think? HAASS: Well, you're old enough, like me, to understand my reference. This is the $64,000 question or maybe, better yet, the 64,000-ruble question. INSKEEP: OK. HAASS: Why would the United States help? Is it a - is it - yeah. We're in the land of speculation here. We have no evidence 'cause it makes no strategic sense. It makes no ethical or moral sense. Maybe he's still mad at President Zelenskyy of Ukraine for not dishing him dirt on President Biden during the - their election campaign. Who knows about the, you know, economic ties to Russia or any other ties? Maybe he's just - finds himself liking or admiring the strongman that is Vladimir Putin. I don't know. We're in the land of speculation. What I do know, what you know, what we all know - anyone listening to this knows - is the United States is tilting towards Russia, away from Ukraine. And that is morally and strategically bankrupt for this country. INSKEEP: Richard Haass, longtime diplomat and former president of the Council on Foreign Relations. Thanks so much. HAASS: Thanks for having me.

items.title: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Here's What Warren Buffett Would Do to Stay Ahead - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Here's What Warren Buffett Would Do to Stay Ahead  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Last month, investing legend Warren Buffett stepped down from his position as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway . This legendary holding company has significantly outperformed the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -1.11% ) in the roughly six decades that he has been in charge, delivering an average annual return of over 19% compared to the market's average of 10%.
But while Buffett is no longer in charge of Berkshire (shifting to a more advisory role as chairman emeritus), investors still look to his wisdom when deciding how to navigate difficult situations. Let's discuss some reasons why the current stock market boom may be on shaky footing and see what lessons Buffett can give to help investors stay ahead.
After a brief dip during the COVID-19 pandemic, stocks have been on a tear, with the S&P 500 delivering an average annual return of 23% between 2022 and 2025. This is mainly due to optimism about a new technology called generative artificial intelligence (AI), which has led to a scramble for expensive data center equipment, resulting in booming growth for the tech giants that design and manufacture it.
The recent performance of AI infrastructure stocks has been nothing short of breathtaking, with top performers like Sandisk up over 1,000% in the last 12 months because of soaring demand for their products. AI-focused data center providers like the recently IPO'd Space Exploration Technologies (aka SpaceX) have also captivated Wall Street's attention.
That said, with a price-to-sales (P/S) multiple of 68 (compared to the S&P 500's average of 3.85), SpaceX shares are extremely expensive, and this might be a sign that excitement is overshadowing reality. The situation seems similar to the dot-com bubble in the late 1990s, when the emergence of the internet led to a similar boom in tech valuations.
Right now, the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of the S&P 500 stands at 41.8. This number is well above its average of 17.4. And the only time it has been higher is in late 1999, when it peaked at 44 shortly before the dot-com bubble turned into a market crash.
In a May interview with CNBC, Buffett criticized the current mood in the stock market, stating, "It's tough to find values when everybody is preferring gambling." Famously cautious, Buffett tends to prefer buying stable and low-priced businesses with easy-to-understand business models. A speculative industry like generative AI isn't his usual cup of tea.
That said, Buffett has limited exposure to the megatrend through diversified, consumer-focused tech giants like Alphabet , Apple , and Amazon rather than pure-play chipmakers. Buffett has also indirectly bet on the "boring" side of the opportunity through investments in utility providers such as MidAmerican Energy and NV Energy, which operate  massive power grids across the Midwest and Nevada. These companies help serve the massive energy demands of AI data centers built in these areas.
Some might credit Buffett's AI strategy to luck instead of skill (many of these investments were made long before the release of ChatGPT). But either way, these picks show how investors can gain exposure to a growth opportunity while minimizing downside risk.
The most interesting thing about Buffett's investing strategy might not be the stocks he buys. Instead, it is what he is not buying. Under his leadership, Berkshire Hathaway has stuck with its stable, profitable technology leaders rather than chasing the biggest returns in less diversified AI stocks that have the furthest to fall if things go south.
Berkshire Hathaway is also sitting on a $365.5 billion cash pile, which will allow it to pursue deals in the event of a market downturn. It might pay to follow Buffett's lead.

items.title: U.S. may have withheld warnings to Ukraine of Russian strikes that killed 6, cut power to 600,000, sources say - CBS News
items.summary: U.S. may have withheld warnings to Ukraine of Russian strikes that killed 6, cut power to 600,000, sources say  CBS News
items.content:
The U.S. may have intentionally withheld early warnings this week of Russian strikes on Ukraine , multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning from our partners" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage at Kyiv and other locations early Tuesday.
The sources said American officials told their Ukrainian counterparts the system used to detect Russian missile launches had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the topic, told CBS News they did not believe the excuse, and they accused the U.S. instead of "playing" with the system.
When Russia launched another wave of ballistic missiles around 3 a.m. local time on Wednesday, the sources said the U.S. early warning system appeared to be working again.
Ukrainian rescuers and paramedics carry a wounded resident at the site of a Russian missile strike on an apartment building in Kyiv, Oct. 14, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
The sources said the U.S. had failed to provide intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches during one previous instance earlier this year, citing the need to focus more resources on the Middle East.
Zelenskyy said Wednesday that Russia launched more than 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions during the overnight attack, primarily targeting energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power.
President Trump, asked Tuesday if the U.S. had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, said: "No, we haven't. We help them, but we're really helping them get to a final answer. We want the war ended."
"We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end," Mr. Trump said.
Russia started launching strikes soon after Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire."
Ukrainian firefighters extinguish a blaze at the site of a Russian missile strike on an apartment building in Kyiv, Oct. 14, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Earlier this week, the Trump administration threatened to stop sharing intelligence and to halt the purchase of U.S.-made weapons by European allies for Ukraine via the PURL procurement system if Ukraine did not stop deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, a European and a Ukrainian official told CBS News.
Ukraine relies on U.S. intelligence for both offensive and defensive military capabilities, including data from satellites and aircraft sensors used to identify launches of Russian aircraft and missiles. Sources familiar with the matter told CBS News the U.S. had not ceased intelligence sharing with Ukraine overall — calling the lack of a warning about this week's attacks a specific incident.
Ukrainian officials and soldiers also told CBS News that Ukraine's military had started experiencing difficulties Tuesday night and Wednesday morning with Starlink, the satellite technology owned by SpaceX's Elon Musk.
In an interview with CBS News earlier this year, Ukraine's former minister of defense Mykhailo Fedorov said Starlink was one of Ukraine's most important technologies, as it allows Ukrainian soldiers to communicate and carry out strikes in environments saturated by electronic warfare.
"On the night of 14 October, without warning the Defence Forces, SpaceX unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals ('military package') while in motion. This complicates UAV missions, particularly interceptors and middle-strike drones, and reduces capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance and signal relay," sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense told CBS News. "At present, the Ministry of Defence is in contact with the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners, is collecting data from all units, and backup communication channels are being tested and put into use."
The Starlink restrictions were first reported by the Kyiv Independent and the Financial Times. CBS News has reached out to SpaceX, the White House, and the Pentagon for comment.
On Wednesday, as President Zelenskyy arrived in the United Kingdom to meet with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other officials, he called for a U.S. response to the recent Russian strikes.
"The strike was absolutely deliberate and indicative in its scale — such a demonstrative disrespect from Russia toward America has never happened before. Russia does not consider the statements of the President of America to be strong," he wrote on X. "We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not close their eyes to reality to respond, and to respond harshly."

Early on Wednesday, Ukraine claimed that SpaceX ( SPCX ) was restricting speed for Starlink satellite internet terminals used by Ukraine amid Russia's ongoing invasion of the country, the Wall Street Journal reported .
"I confirm that SpaceX implemented a speed limit for Starlink terminals operating in motion last night," said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, according to WSJ. "Our defense forces received no warning about this restriction, and it has led to the disruption of a number of missions."
Starlink, essentially a global broadband internet service delivered from space, is a core part of SpaceX's business . There are more than 10 million Starlink subscribers worldwide, and SpaceX is now moving to challenge legacy wireless carriers.
A Ukrainian serviceman of the 47th Brigade prepares a Starlink satellite internet system at the frontline. (Reuters/Inna Varenytsia/File Photo) · Reuters / REUTERS Ukrainian military drone crews and logistics operations regularly leverage Starlink to provide video feeds and precise targeting. On Wednesday afternoon, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk stated that SpaceX was not involved in the latest decision to restrict those specific services.
A senior US official then told Barik Ravid of Axios that the Trump administration had nothing to do with any Starlink service constraints.
In any case, this is not the first time Ukraine has experienced Starlink throttling, though it is the first since SpaceX became a public company this summer.
In 2022, as Ukraine retook territory from Russia, Musk reportedly ordered SpaceX engineers to cut some Starlink coverage in contested areas of Ukraine. In 2023, the company acknowledged efforts to throttle Starlink usage during the war.
"There are things that we can do to limit their ability to [leverage Starlink]," Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and COO, said at the time. "There are things that we can do, and have done."
Musk is an ally of President Trump, who has recently ramped up criticism of Zelensky. Ukraine also bombed Russian data centers recently, disrupting bot traffic on Musk-owned X and other social media platforms.
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who is not running for reelection and supports the US backing Ukraine's defense, posted on X — which Musk owns — seeking clarification on SpaceX's policy related to Starlink services.

items.title: Germany shifts toward tougher EU trade defenses as pressure from Chinese competition grows - DW.com
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Germany and France are pushing for stronger EU trade defense tools amid rising Chinese competition Image: DW Advertisement
Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's   unfair trade practices.
In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt  German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.
Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market  if unfair practices continue.
Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means." 
China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction." 
Before the COVID pandemic , the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent .
Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.
Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking , precision engineering and chemicals industries.
German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.
Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of  layoffs and possible factory closures .
VW, Audi and Porsche have announced workforce reductions totaling tens of thousands of jobs as the industry undergoes a huge transformation Image: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance
In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.
"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.
Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."
Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:
"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.
According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.
While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.
Business groups question industrial policy proposals
The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.
Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.
How to dismantle China's stranglehold on raw materials?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."
Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.
Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on how many hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report. 
Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.
Reports say the agreement would cap such Chinese imports at 350,000 vehicles annually, with the limit increasing by 6% each year over four years.
Amid intense Chinese rivalry, the EU says it wants to restore industrial production in Europe Image: Torsten Krüger/imageBROKER/picture alliance Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.
MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion (€354 billion), versus $172 billion to the US.
This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.
"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.

items.content:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham in London. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters Pool/AP
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham in London. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters Pool/AP
Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access
Ukrainian president accused US president of picking the other side over four years of war
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite squeezed, raising doubts about long-term US support for Kyiv.
The Ukrainian president, on a visit to London, accused Trump of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in relations already strained by the US agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow .
Ahead of a meeting with prime minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street, Zelenskyy appeared in a TV interview where he was asked whether the sudden restriction of Starlink was deliberate and if he felt betrayed by Trump.
“Really, yes … but it’s a little bit more complicated ⁠than just my emotions or my feelings,” the Ukrainian president replied, adding: “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner.”
Overnight, Ukraine’s military reported that, without explanation, the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph .
That effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable – and, it later emerged, affected the most effective air defence system to stop Russian jet-powered attack drones bombing Kyiv.
“I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.”
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.
The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say the closure of the strait of Hormuz after the US-Israel attack on Iran has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
Andy Burnham greeted Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warmly at No 10. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters The two leaders fell out in the spring of 2025 during a disastrous visit by Zelenskyy to the Oval Office, where the US president said: “You don’t have the cards” to win the war. The row was followed by a brief pause in intelligence sharing and a desperate scramble by European allies to calm the row.
Burnham met Zelenskyy in Downing Street on Wednesday, hours after he promised MPs that the Ukrainian president “would not leave empty-handed” and that he had tasked officials with drawing up further sanctions and options for speeding up military aid.
As the pair met at No 10, he promised that Britain’s support for Ukraine would remain constant. “You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change,” he said.
Zelenskyy had met King Charles in Buckingham Palace earlier on Wednesday.
In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
In brief remarks to reporters, Zelenskyy said he hoped to raise access to Starlink and intelligence sharing in his meeting with the British prime minister.
Burnham pledged that he would accelerate the supply of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which the country uses to counter Russian drone strikes and said they were looking for “all possible avenues” of further support.
The prime minister also said he was prepared to discuss the ceasefire proposed by Trump on attacks on energy infrastructure but acknowledged that Moscow had not abided by it.
“Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said.
Earlier Burnham told MPs at PMQs that he wanted to be “careful” about potential criticism of Trump that might risk exacerbating tensions, saying he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation: “I will listen to President Zelenskyy carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.”
The meeting, which lasted just over an hour, began as Burnham greeted Zelenskyy with a hug on Downing Street, before the pair walked to the door of No 10 and posed for photographs, flanked by Irish Guards in full ceremonial uniform.
Musk said the decision to curtail Starlink was not one made by him. The communications system is not directly licensed to clients who are using weapons, and the Ukrainian military was linked to a related network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Trump.
Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser on military technology to Zelenskyy, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
The Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechanging | Editorial
Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.
“With their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.
It also complicates Ukraine’s use of medium-range, mid-strike drones for hitting targets in its territories occupied by Russia. But, ironically, it would have no impact on Ukraine’s deep strike bombing of oil refineries because Kyiv is banned from using Starlink to hit targets inside of Russia.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become more widespread.
Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”

items.title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
items.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan had worked for the AI giant for more than a year before he was arrested by the FBI.
items.content:
Image caption, A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".
As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.
The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).
Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.
Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".
The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.
Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.
The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.
Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.
But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.
On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.
A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.
The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.
When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.
In a post on X , external , OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".
It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."
Image caption, Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been inserted
Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.
Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.
"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."
Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."
On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (Â£190,000) fine.

items.title: Microsoft Just Unveiled a Brand-New AI Chip. Could It Be the "Nvidia Killer" Everyone's Been Looking For? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Microsoft Just Unveiled a Brand-New AI Chip. Could It Be the "Nvidia Killer" Everyone's Been Looking For?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
On Monday, Microsoft ( MSFT -1.80% ) unveiled its latest AI chip architecture, the Maia 300.
And the company went out of its way to point out the ways in which the Maia 300 was superior to graphics processing units (GPUs). "This is our biggest bet yet on our own silicon," said CEO Satya Nadella.
This was seen as a shot across the bow to the world's premier GPU maker, Nvidia ( NVDA -3.16% ) .
So is the Maia 300 the "Nvidia killer" that everyone has been anticipating for years? It might be, but not in the way you might think. Here's what's really going on.
The Maia 300 is an upgraded version of the Maia 200, which was released in January.
The Maia 200 is currently in production and has already been deployed at Microsoft facilities in Iowa and Arizona, where it's used instead of GPUs and other components from Nvidia, Intel ( INTC -4.56% ) , and Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD -5.73% ) .
Microsoft claims the new, upgraded Maia 300 chip is even more economical and can process 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared to GPUs. A higher token-per-megawatt ratio results in lower AI costs because the biggest expense for an AI data center is electricity.
But even if it's cheaper to operate, it's certainly not going to match the power of Nvidia's top-of-the-line systems. Won't that be an issue?
Perhaps more than any other company, Microsoft has done very well by coming in second. Its Azure cloud platform is the second-largest , compared to Amazon 's Amazon Web Services. Its Surface tablets have never outsold Apple 's iPad. Its Xbox has always played second fiddle to the Sony PlayStation.
So it shouldn't surprise anyone that Microsoft isn't trying to beat Nvidia at its own game, but to compete on a more favorable playing field: cost. "Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems," Microsoft said in its blog post announcing the Maia 300 system. The company hopes to leverage this to its advantage.
Austin Lyons, an analyst for Chipstrat, thinks there's an opportunity here in optimizing different AI processors for different tasks. "The advantage of custom silicon is that Microsoft can optimize for the latency its own workloads actually require," he wrote. "A meeting summary and a coding agent don't need the same response time. Maia targets more throughput at each of those latency points, translates to more useful tokens served per megawatt and lower cost passed for customers."
Pat Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy agrees, writing:
Microsoft is now moving toward deploying Maia at meaningful production scale. At that scale, custom silicon isn't just about performance. It can become an important margin driver by improving the economics of delivering Microsoft's own AI services.
Lyons and Moorhead are echoing commentary from across the industry that suggests the AI race is evolving away from a zero-sum contest to create the fastest, most powerful processors. Hyperscalers and other major players are starting to think about the economics of AI and what customers will be willing to pay in an era where the tech giants start to monetize the new technology.
By running lower-difficulty, in-house AI queries on processors that operate more cheaply, Microsoft is taking another step in proactive cost management, which is one of the key reasons investors rewarded the stock earlier this year.

So while the Maia 300 isn't an Nvidia killer on its own, it's evidence that the most powerful AI processors -- currently Nvidia's GPUs -- may not be everyone's universal first choice in the future for every application. Routing an AI query to the cheapest infrastructure possible for the difficulty of the problem presented may become the norm.
In other words, even if Nvidia continues to produce the best tech in the world for decades to come, its sales volume might suffer regardless.
The Maia 300 doesn't even begin production until sometime in 2027. And even then, Nvidia AI infrastructure is almost certain to remain a critical part of Microsoft's AI mix.
Just last week, Microsoft started taking preorders for a new Surface Laptop Ultra with a starting price of $2,599. That hefty price tag is thanks to its powerful processor that can run AI models without requiring cloud access.
The maker of that incredibly powerful chip? You guessed it: Nvidia.

items.title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
items.summary: Four years after the attacks, Serhii Kuznetsov appears in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany.
items.content:
Image caption, Serhii Kuznetsov (C) was pictured in court on Wednesday as the trial got under way
By Jessica Parker ,Â  Berlin correspondent in Hamburg Â  and Â  Paul Kirby ,Â  Europe digital editor
A Ukrainian man has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany, four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history.
Prosecutors say Serhii Kuznetsov played a leading role in a team of saboteurs that destroyed the pipelines, accusing him of a war crime. His defence has called for the case to be dismissed.
The case is highly sensitive in Germany, one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.
Extradited to Germany last year, Kuznetsov denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.
Kuznetsov became the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts on Wednesday morning, and a packed public gallery looked on as he entered the courtroom, appearing relaxed.
He even smiled at times, including during initial exchanges where he spoke to confirm personal details such as his name and place of birth.
He had previously only been identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K and pictured with his face blurred, but a court spokeswoman said he had now waived his anonymity.
Kuznetsov, 50, wore a pair of headphones and appeared to listen intently to a translation of proceedings in Ukrainian, as the prosecution read out the charges against him of ordering divers and an explosive expert to attack civilian infrastructure.
The defence outlined their case, telling the court that only circumstantial evidence had emerged in the four years since the Nord Stream blasts.
"[Prosecutors] made a thorough investigation of four years," Italian defence lawyer Nicola Canestrini told the BBC outside the courtroom. "They did not find one single witness, they did not find no forensics, no DNA, no fingerprints - nothing!"
Image caption, Kuznetsov was extradited to Germany from Italy late last year
Canestrini and his colleagues argued that as a soldier the defendant was bound to secrecy, and therefore he could not have a fair trial as he was unable to defend himself.
"Let's say he has an alibi, he was on another secret operation, how can you prove that if he's [not able] to tell us as defence attorneys where he was and which witnesses we could summon?"
Prosecutors argue the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime, as an "attack by military means against civilian objects".
The defence told the court his extradition to Germany was flawed as no mention had been made at the time of the war crime allegation.
In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.
Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.
As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied.
Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock.
They said later that "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat".
Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction , external and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security".
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies".
Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin.
Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war".
He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."
However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.
"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.
Image caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022
In August 2025, Kuznetsov was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.
After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, when his surname emerged in court documents, Kuznetsov was transferred to Germany late last year.
German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army , external , and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.
While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.
In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".
Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.
Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.
Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

items.title: Are the European Women's World Cup play-offs working?
items.summary: The ease in which England saw off Greece in round one of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs showed just how inefficient the structure currently is.
items.content:
Image caption, England have lost just once this year but have still not qualified for the 2027 Women's World Cup
The ease in which England saw off Greece in round one of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs showed just how inefficient the structure currently is.
The two-time European champions were superior in every sense as they won 8-1 on aggregate against a Greece side ranked 55 places lower in the world.
Realistically, Greece stood little chance in a two-legged tie against Sarina Wiegman's side despite performing well in their home 3-1 defeat.
England's resounding victory was not a one-off as Europe's other top nations, who were forced to drop into the play-offs, also met lower-ranked opposition and won emphatically.
It was not an evening that truly reflects the growth of European women's football, which has become more competitive than ever in recent years.
It was, however, indicative that the qualification process perhaps needs reviewing by Uefa.
'Unplayable' Stanway a free-scoring warrior for Lionesses
One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification.
The Netherlands, 2017 European champions, finished second in their group behind France, ranked sixth in the world. They went on to beat Hungary 11-0 on aggregate.
Norway, World Cup winners in 1995 and six-time European finalists, lost out to giants Germany in their group and ended up beating Romania 8-0.
Other League A fallouts Sweden and the Republic of Ireland thrashed their opponents 15-0 and 12-0 respectively.
So it was no surprise when back-to-back European champions England, who were drawn in the same group as world champions Spain, went on to record another heavy victory against much weaker opposition from League C in their play-off.
"Of course we wanted to qualify straight away, that's not the case," said England manager Wiegman when asked about the qualification process again on Tuesday.
"For us now, the facts are that we are in the play-offs, we have played Greece, now we're through, and now we're going to play Ukraine. That's what my focus is on.
"Uefa will review how things are set up and see whether they think it works or it should be better, or different. I don't think it's my place now to review that."
The Lionesses still have another two-legged tie against Ukraine to play, with the first leg taking place away from home on 1 December and the return fixture at Wembley Stadium on 5 December.
Ukraine are a side who England beat twice in the league phase by an aggregate score of 9-1.
It seems absurd that they should have to beat the same team on at least three occasions as part of their qualification process.
England have won seven of their last eight qualifying matches, scoring 21 goals, conceding just six times, and their only defeat was away from home against world champions Spain.
They came runners-up in League A3 only on their head-to-head record with the best team in the world - they even beat Spain 1-0 at Wembley.
England's overall tally of 15 points in the league phase was beaten by just three other teams - Germany, Switzerland and Hungary.
Switzerland and Hungary were also in qualifying groups in League B and League C that did not include a single team from the world's top 45 ranked nations.
In contrast England, who were seeded in League A, had Iceland - ranked 13th - as a tricky opponent, and world number one Spain in their four-team group.
Image caption, There were several heavy aggregate results in European qualifying
When qualifying for the 2023 Women's World Cup, England beat Latvia on two occasions, winning 20-0 and 10-0 .
That tournament saw an increase from 24 to 32 teams and while qualification was still one-sided, the showpiece in Australia and New Zealand was a different story.
England were tested against debutants Haiti in the group stages, narrowly winning 1-0, and by Colombia in their quarter-final, despite the South American side failing to qualify for the previous tournament.
The level of competition was growing and it was evident even more so across Europe with England failing to qualify for the 2024 Olympic Games on behalf of Team GB after finishing second to the Netherlands in their Nations League group.
A draw with Portugal and defeat by Belgium were suffered by England the following year, while they were forced to overcome two penalty shootouts in Euro 2025.
There is no denying that England's competition has improved but they were still dealt a rough hand in this year's World Cup qualifying campaign.
Following their costly 4-0 defeat by Spain in June, Wiegman said: "The competition in Europe is really high.
"What I'm disappointed about is that we win five games, we have 15 points and we're in a group with the world champions and then you can't qualify.
"I'm happy with the performances but not the result of us having to go into the play-offs. That's just the way it is."
What is frustrating for England is that while they picked up a routine win over Greece and now prepare to face an opponent they have already played twice in 2026, their potential World Cup rivals are getting to play matches against top-tier teams.
Two of the tournament favourites Germany and Japan met in a friendly match on Tuesday night; Brazil and Argentina played out a 2-2 draw and four-time world champions USA played Spain twice in five days in a mouth-watering meeting.
Fifa has announced that the 2031 Women's World Cup will be expanded from 32 to 48 teams and it is too early to know if that is the right decision.
But while larger scorelines remain, it is clear it is more a direct result of a European qualification process that doesn't benefit the majority.

The Aiguille du Midi cable car traverses the slopes of Mont-Blanc in Haute-Savoie, France. Photograph: Design Pics Inc/Alamy
Mont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a year
Peak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climate
Western Europe’s highest mountain shrank by more than a metre last year. The peak of Mont Blanc in France now stands 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors said on Wednesday, putting “the roof of Europe” 1.29 metres lower than in 2025.
The mountain is about 4,792 metres tall but the summit constantly shifts as heat, wind and precipitation change the thickness of snow and ice on top. The height scientists recorded during an expedition last month was 1.88 metres greater than it was in 2023, when it reached the lowest levels in recent memory.
Chartered surveyors from the Union Nationale des Géomètres-Experts (UNGE) and the Ordre des Géomètres-Experts, who have regularly monitored the peak since 2001, used precise satellite technology to measure the mountain, and drones to create a detailed model of the snow and ice cap.
The summit has shrunk back by 3.43 metres since a high of 4,810.90 metres in 2007, the data shows.
The experts cautioned against linking fluctuations in height from year to year to the rapid loss of Alpine ice being caused by fossil fuel pollution.
“Regarding ice mass, it is essential to distinguish between changes in surface altitude and changes in the total volume or mass of ice,” a UNGE spokesperson said. “An increase in summit altitude does not necessarily mean that the mountain has gained ice mass, nor does it contradict the documented retreat of Alpine glaciers.”
Climate breakdown was a factor in western Europe’s hottest summer on record this year, scarring Alpine regions and melting ice at dizzying speed. Earlier this month, Swiss glaciologists warned of an “ explosion of melt rates ” after confirming that one-fifth of the country’s ice had been lost in the past five years, and 5.5% of volume was lost between 2025 and 2026.
Jean des Garets, the president of the Haute-Savoie departmental chamber of surveyors and the leader of the Mont Blanc expedition, said the warming trend could be seen with the naked eye in the rest of the Alpine massif but that “for the moment, climate change doesn’t seem to have the same impact above 4,000 metres”.
“When we climb, we pass by the Brigade Blanche hut before the Tête-Rousse glacier,” he said in comments reported by the French television channel TF1 on Wednesday. “We’ve seen that the glacier has moved up. It has literally melted before our very eyes and now in some places we’re crossing a stream instead of a glacier.”
