items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Share Iran targets Starlink as ‘tool of war’ with hints of more internet curbs on social media
The use of satellite-based internet services and the distribution of Starlink terminals are subject to fines and imprisonment in Iran [File: Pierre Crom/Getty Images]
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have pledged to continue a crackdown against satellite internet service Starlink, along with further restrictions on the global internet as the US-Israel war on Iran continues.
Elon Musk’s Starlink, which is free of the heavy filtering and restrictions imposed by Tehran, is outlawed in Iran on national security grounds. The use of satellite-based internet services and the distribution of Starlink terminals are subject to fines and imprisonment.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 SpaceX’s showpiece Starship rocket reaches orbit for first time
list 2 of 3 ‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan?
list 3 of 3 Poland says two Turks arrested over Russia-linked Starlink station fire
It is one of the many measures imposed by Iranian authorities since the United States and Israel launched strikes on the country on February 28, leading to a prolonged and economically punishing war between the countries.
Iran’s 90 million people have undergone two lengthy state-imposed global internet shutdowns in 2026 – for three weeks during nationwide protests in January and for 88 days at the start of the ongoing war .
Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, secretary of the Supreme National Cyberspace Council, described Starlink as a “tool of war” for enemies.
“It is a tool used for command and control by the enemy, for espionage and information gathering,” he said. “We have several systems for cutting off Starlink satellite terminals.”
He did not elaborate on what measures or devices were being used to block Starlink, but one was deployed during the January protests and authorities were prepared to share the technology with aligned countries.
Iran is among several countries that have banned or restricted Starlink due to national security concerns.
It has set baseline sentences of between six months and two years for using or possessing Starlink. Importing and distributing the devices carry jail terms of up to five years. If paired with national security or espionage charges, individuals can even face the death penalty.
Aghamiri has called on Iranians to use domestic platforms, supported by what the authorities call the National Information Network. He also backed a  tiered-access model, which envisages protected international access for selected groups – such as traders, researchers and journalists – during periods of internet restrictions.
A Tehran-based internet and telecommunications expert, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Al Jazeera that Iranian authorities use a combination of measures to block Starlink connections.
This includes the use of multiple jammers with different configurations to disrupt services, along with spoofed GPS locations to slow new devices being set up. They can also identify Starlink-associated internet protocols if they connect to local applications and services.
Authorities also try to physically intercept terminals using patrols and drone searches, or raid locations selling the terminals.
In June, Israeli politician Naftali Bennett claimed that Israel had smuggled tens of thousands of Starlink devices into Iran when he was prime minister, between 2021 and 2022, to aid antigovernment protesters.
Since 2023, Iran has also pursued the matter at the International Telecommunication Union’s Radio Regulations Board, trying to pressure the US and Norway, which plays a role in the satellite network’s regulatory filings, to halt transmissions.
On October 4, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned the Norwegian ambassador in Tehran to protest against what it described as a failure to act over unauthorised Starlink operations.
During a governance meeting at the end of September, Deputy Technology Minister Mohammad Hafez Hakami had warned authorities that Starlink could signify “the last nail in the coffin of the [cyberspace] governance” of Iran if it becomes prevalent, due to the unfettered internet access it provides.
He pointed out that the government blocked the messaging app Telegram after the cost-of-living protests in 2017-18, but had to resort to a weeklong internet shutdown for the first time during the nationwide protests in 2019 . WhatsApp and Instagram were blocked after the 2022-23 protests, which preceded the near-total shutdown during the January 2026 protests.
“If this trend continues, in the next crisis we will have to cut electricity, because Starlink, as a new tool of evading state governance, is fundamentally not even dependent on our network,” Hakami said.
Starlink has allowed Iranians to send out videos of the protests abroad since 2022 despite state restrictions. Tens of thousands of terminals are believed to have been smuggled into the country since, but exact figures are unknown.
Due to the risk of a state crackdown, limited availability and financial costs, most people still have no access to Starlink and must rely on Iran’s domestic internet, which blocks most international services and thousands of websites. US sanctions and banking restrictions further impede Iranians’ access to global services.
To circumvent the many roadblocks, most Iranians use virtual private networks (VPNs) and other methods that grant access to the free internet. But those tools can reduce connection speeds, prove costly or provide unsafe connections that jeopardise user data, and become harder to come by during periods of state-imposed internet blackout.
According to the authorities, more restrictions were possible in the future if the war intensifies, after a relative decrease in violence since the June memorandum of understanding, which eventually lapsed without a permanent ceasefire, between the US and Iran.
Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani told a news conference on Tuesday that state bodies were deliberately disrupting the internet ostensibly to protect people and national assets from cyberattacks.
“It is obvious that due to the importance of our databases and internet-based services, decision-making bodies are sometimes forced to bring down internet speeds,” she said. “We don’t deny this issue.”
The authorities claim that they have considered removing restrictions on some platforms, although no action has been taken yet.
State-linked media late on Tuesday released a policy and governance framework document that the cyberspace council’s Aghamiri said has been under consideration for nearly two years but remained confidential due to security concerns.
The document offered no timeline for reopening any platform, and media reports said implementation had been halted by wars and protests.
The document says Google Play and WhatsApp could potentially be unblocked, while YouTube and Telegram would have to negotiate with Iran and accept certain conditions determined by the authorities to be unblocked. Such steps by the social media giants are considered extremely unlikely.

items.title: Diesel squeeze set to last well into 2027 as Iran war disrupts supply, IEA says - CNBC
items.summary: Diesel squeeze set to last well into 2027 as Iran war disrupts supply, IEA says &nbs
items.content:
Diesel squeeze to last until 2027 as Iran war disrupts supply: IEA
The IEA said replenishing lost inventories may not begin before the second half of 2027, even as refinery output recovers.
Diesel exports fell by 700,000 barrels a day year on year in September, while wholesale prices reached record highs in several major markets.
The IEA said the proposed Russian diesel supply deal would have little macroeconomic impact, and warned that renewed Gulf attacks could derail the oil supply recovery.
A garbage truck drives past gas prices above $6 a gallon and diesel prices above $8 a gallon as they are displayed outside of a Shell gas station in Carson, California on September 22, 2026.
Constraints on the diesel market will extend well into next year, the International Energy Agency warned on Wednesday.
In its October Oil Market Report, the IEA said supply would remain tight into the latter half of 2027.
A counter-seasonal tightening in gasoil markets in the third quarter, combined with "much heavier-than-normal inventory declines" in the preceding three months, had "deprived global gasoil markets of crucial stock cover ahead of the peak winter demand season," the IEA said.
Last month saw global diesel exports drop by 700,000 barrels a day year-on-year, according to IEA data. A 1.3 million barrels per day loss from Russia and the Middle East was "only partly offset by higher supply from other sources," the agency said.
But while higher prices had weakened oil demand more broadly, the IEA said "relatively price inelastic diesel demand has remained strong," supported by government measures aimed at easing high prices for consumers.
"Falling inventories, soaring cracks, and steepening levels of backwardation have signalled the need for additional supplies," it said. "However, even with a rapid recovery expected in refinery throughputs into year-end, gasoil supply falls short of meeting demand in 4Q26, suggesting that the replenishment of lost inventories, outside of typical seasonal fluctuations, is unlikely before [the second half of 2027]."
The IEA pointed out that wholesale diesel prices exceeded $200 a barrel in Singapore in mid-September and reached all-time highs of around $220 per barrel in Europe and the United States.
"Retail diesel prices have risen in tandem to record levels in most major economies," it said in its report. But it warned that tensions in the crude freight market meant delivered diesel prices in the dominant gasoil importing markets – Europe, Africa and Latin America – could rise again in the coming weeks.
Trump strikes Russian diesel deal to ease consumer squeeze
U.S. diesel prices hit $6 a gallon for the first time last month, as the Iran war continued to impact global energy markets, with some market watchers warning elevated prices could linger for months to come.
Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had made a deal with Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin for Russia to immediately supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the global market, in a bid to offset sharp price rises sparked by Iran war-driven supply constraints.
Russian diesel exports loading from the Baltic port of Primorsk resumed on Tuesday, with a tanker carrying around 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel heading towards Morocco, according to LSEG data reported by Reuters on Wednesday.
Trump's diesel deal with Russia equals less than two weeks of U.S. demand
Trump turns to Russian diesel ahead of midterms, but analysts see little price relief
More Republicans come out against Trump's diesel deal with Putin
Russian energy has been harshly sanctioned by Western governments since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Trump's deal with Putin faced bipartisan condemnation in the U.S., with lawmakers in Europe also criticizing the move. Speaking at the IMF meetings in Bangkok on Wednesday, Valdis Dombrovskis, European Commissioner for the Economy and Productivity, warned "now is not a time to ease sanctions on Russia."
"If we discuss this diesel deal specifically, it's worth noting that the volumes which are being discussed are anyway not going to have any macroeconomic significance, and the big question mark if Russia is able to deliver them anyway," he said.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Wednesday warned the deal contradicts efforts to get Putin to the negotiating table with Ukraine.
Brent crude continues to top $100 a barrel amid conflict-related supply disruption
The IEA forecast that overall oil demand would fall by an average of 2.6 million barrels per day in 2026. Diesel will register 25% of that demand drop, the agency said.
Oil supply, meanwhile, was forecast to post an average annual decline of 5.8 million barrels per day this year, before reversing course to rise by 7.7 million barrels per day in 2027.
However, the IEA warned that "renewed attacks in the Gulf leave the recovery fragile."

items.title: Not Nvidia. Not Micron. This Under-the-Radar Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chip Stock Could Be the Biggest Winner in 2027. - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Not Nvidia. Not Micron. This Under-the-Radar Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chip Stock Could Be the Biggest Winner in 2027.  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Nvidia ( NVDA -3.16% ) and Micron Technology ( MU -4.08% ) are two of the stock market's biggest artificial intelligence (AI) success stories. Nvidia dominates AI accelerators, while Micron is benefiting from extraordinary demand for memory chips. Both companies have delivered remarkable growth, rewarding investors who recognized their opportunities early.
But as Wall Street looks toward 2027, another semiconductor stock could be preparing for its breakout moment. Marvell Technology ( MRVL -8.72% ) has already rallied on enthusiasm surrounding custom AI chips and advanced networking.
However, the company's latest investor day projections, a lucrative partnership with Nvidia, and an expanding relationship with Alphabet  suggest something more substantial than hype. As investors look beyond the obvious AI winners, Marvell could attract considerably more attention.
Marvell isn't trying to replace Nvidia's GPUs or compete with Micron's memory solutions. Instead, the company focuses on two increasingly important components of AI infrastructure: custom silicon and high-speed connectivity.
Custom accelerators allow hyperscalers to design processors specifically optimized for certain workloads. Meanwhile, optical networking and interconnect technologies help move enormous quantities of data between chips, servers, and data centers.
During its recent investor day conference, Marvell estimated its total addressable market (TAM) could approach $400 billion by calendar 2030. Management outlined approximately $37 billion in interconnect revenue and roughly $30 billion from custom silicon by fiscal year 2031. This forecast reflects expectations for annualized growth of approximately 65% and 80%, respectively, across the two businesses.

Back in March, Nvidia invested $2 billion in Marvell. The deal helped establish a strategic partnership focused on connecting custom AI processors with Nvidia's computing and networking ecosystem. The relationship focuses on NVLink Fusion, which allows AI developers to integrate specialized processors into Nvidia-based racks.
This is important because it positions Marvell as a beneficiary of the broader data center build-out rather than simply a competitor to Nvidia. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's willingness to invest in Marvell provides a meaningful endorsement of its technology.
In addition, Marvell's expanding relationship with Alphabet involves developing custom silicon supporting Google Cloud's AI infrastructure, including chips that complement its Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) ecosystem.
Specifically, Google received warrants tied to as much as $120 billion in potential chip purchases through fiscal 2033. While this isn't guaranteed revenue, it still illustrates the enormous scale of the relationship and the importance of Marvell's position in the AI chip value chain.
For years, memory and storage were viewed as commodity products. For this reason, memory stocks have had to fend off a narrative that they operate in cyclical markets. As AI infrastructure spending continues accelerating, investors are starting to realize that GPUs were only part of the equation. Memory and storage are now essential bottlenecks, sending shares of companies like Micron and Sandisk soaring.
Marvell could experience a similar shift in investor perception in 2027. The reason boils down to how AI spending is evolving. Hyperscalers aren't simply procuring more GPUs. They're building increasingly complex accelerated computing systems that require faster networking, greater bandwidth, and specialized processors designed for particular workloads.
As generative models become more sophisticated and inference deployments expand into new applications, efficiently moving data between processors becomes increasingly important. This is precisely where Marvell's optical networking, interconnect technologies, and custom silicon expertise converge.
Unlike some semiconductor companies waiting for future design wins, Marvell already has major customer programs underway. To get a grasp of how these relationships are impacting Marvell, consider that the company raised its fiscal 2028 revenue target from $18 billion to $20 billion. Importantly, Marvell's fiscal 2028 begins in early 2027 and ends in January 2028 -- meaning the majority of this projected growth will unfold during calendar 2027. Looking even further ahead, management expects total revenue of $70 billion to $90 billion in fiscal 2031. At the midpoint, that's nearly 10 times what Marvell generated during fiscal 2026.
This growth trajectory is why 2027 could represent the inflection point for Marvell. Nvidia has already established itself as the dominant platform for AI factories. Meanwhile, Micron continues to demonstrate the importance of high bandwidth memory and advanced DRAM. Marvell is approaching a period where its own revenue growth could make the importance of connectivity and custom silicon impossible to overlook. For growth investors looking for the next AI semiconductor breakout story, I consider Marvell stock an attractive long-term buy.
